extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and readers interested in narrative structure (especially Western writers/readers unfamiliar with kishotenketsu)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and guidance on using the kishotenketsu four-act structure (ki, sho, ten, ketsu) in storytelling, showing how plot can move without a traditional conflict act. Includes examples (poetry and the film Your Name) to illustrate each act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kishotenketsu — four-act plot structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Kishotenketsu is a four-act plot structure common in Asian storytelling: the introduction (ki), the development (sho), the twist (ten), and the conclusion (ketsu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General framing: unlike many Western narratives, a dedicated conflict act is missing; the structure relies on buildup and a change in direction rather than a central conflict. Useful to think of the structure as sequence: establish, develop, change perspective, and tie together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ki — introduction (kiku in Chinese)
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction (kiku) is the setting: presentation of the characters, era… the important components of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use the ki to establish who the characters are and the world they inhabit. Example from Your Name: introduces Taki and Mitsuha and establishes they have never met. In short forms, the first verse/line can serve this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sho — development
rubrics_metrics.description: The development (shoku) is where the narrative advances. The events of your story start to unfold, setting action in motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use the sho to show how characters interact with the setup and to build relationships or ongoing situations. Example from Your Name: the body-swap episodes and the notes they leave, which build mutual understanding and drive the story until the swap stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten — twist (tenku)
rubrics_metrics.description: The twist (tenku) is when things get interesting: it changes the direction of the plot and presents the story in a new light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key evaluative point: the ten creates the narrative shift that moves the plot forward; it may or may not be an inciting incident ("Can the twist be caused by an inciting incident? Yes. But it is not always the case."). Example: in Your Name the discovery that Mitsuha was a casualty of a past tragedy reframes the story and redirects stakes (romance → saving a town). Assess stories by whether the third act reorients reader priorities rather than escalating a central conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ketsu — conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusion (ketsu) is the end of the story. It usually ties the two directions together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use the ketsu to reconcile or juxtapose the perspectives set up in ki/sho with the reorientation of ten. Example from Your Name: the conclusion centers on maintaining the connection across the changed circumstances and attempting to prevent the tragedy, tying together earlier personal and later communal stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a dedicated conflict act; plot movement by juxtaposition/shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Compared to more familiar narratives, the conflict act is missing in kishotenketsu — it is not the story that lacks conflict, but its structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft/evaluation note: when judging whether a work follows kishotenketsu, look for movement driven by a change of perspective or juxtaposition (ten) rather than by escalation from an inciting incident. The twist should reframe priorities and stakes, steering the reader toward different concerns rather than simply raising tension in the same line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to short forms (shichigon-zekku / Qiyán jueju)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short poetic forms often exemplify kishotenketsu: each line/verse can represent one act (introduction, development, twist, conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: the provided Japanese poem maps four verses to ki/sho/ten/ketsu (introduce characters → develop them → present a contrasting war image → conclude by reframing the characters as dangerous). Use short forms to practice tight, juxtaposed shifts and concise conclusions.
